Symptom severity for the dosing tables: mild = discomfort noticed, no disruption of normal daily activity; moderate = discomfort sufficient to reduce or affect normal daily activity; severe = incapacitating, unable to work or perform normal daily activity (Leqembi PI Table 3 footnote, p.7; Kisunla PI Table 2 footnote, p.6)
Lecanemab: baseline; after 1 month (before 3rd IV or 5th SC dose), 2, 3 and 6 months; MRI within about 1 week before the next dose (Leqembi PI §2.4, p.6)
Enhanced clinical vigilance for ARIA during the first 14 weeks (Leqembi PI §5.1, p.13)
The lecanemab AUR schedule (5th, 7th, 14th infusion) is older than the current label; not used here
Donanemab: baseline; before infusions 2, 3, 4 and 7 (Kisunla PI §2.3, p.5)
Enhanced clinical vigilance for ARIA during the first 24 weeks (Kisunla PI §5.1, p.11)

indication: ARIA on MRI, symptomatic or not
notes: AUR: monthly noncontrast MRI until ARIA-E resolves and ARIA-H stabilizes (lecanemab AUR p.10; donanemab AUR §5.4, p.10; ASNR 2025 p.27)
Label: consider a follow-up MRI 2 to 4 months after initial identification (Leqembi PI Tables 3 and 4, p.7; Kisunla PI Tables 2 and 3, p.6)

decisionRules.condition: Stroke-like deficit on lecanemab or donanemab
decisionRules.recommendation: Consider whether the symptoms could be due to ARIA-E before giving a thrombolytic. For IVT, see vascular-antithrombotics:thrombolysis-with-prior-antithrombotics.
evidenceNote: Label warning, not graded (Leqembi PI §5.1, p.11; Kisunla PI §5.1, p.10)
AHA 2026 Table 8 is not restated here

decisionRules.condition: Acute stroke on lecanemab or donanemab (AUR, stricter than the labels)
decisionRules.recommendation: Lecanemab AUR: no acute thrombolytics. Donanemab AUR: no IVT without a pre-treatment MRI unequivocally excluding ARIA; consider thrombectomy without a thrombolytic for large-vessel occlusion.
May continue dosing (Kisunla: at current dose and schedule).
evidenceNote: Label dosing table; both AURs agree (Leqembi PI Table 3, pp.6–7; Kisunla PI Table 2, pp.5–6; lecanemab AUR p.10; donanemab AUR Table 8, p.11)

decisionRules.condition: ARIA-E mild on MRI with mild symptoms (label)
decisionRules.recommendation: May continue dosing based on clinical judgment.
evidenceNote: Leqembi PI Table 3, p.7; Kisunla PI Table 2, p.6
The AURs are more conservative: see the next rule

decisionRules.condition: ARIA with mild or moderate symptoms, or radiographically moderate ARIA (AUR). Includes the case the label lets you continue: mild ARIA-E with mild symptoms
decisionRules.recommendation: Suspend dosing.
evidenceNote: Lecanemab AUR p.10: moderate or severe radiographic ARIA, or symptoms, suspend; Table 8, p.30

Donanemab AUR §5.4, p.10: suspend if symptomatic or radiographically moderate. The AUR notes the label allows continuing with mild symptoms and mild ARIA-E and says it recommends a slightly more conservative approach. Table 8, p.11

decisionRules.condition: ARIA-E moderate or severe on MRI, or moderate or severe symptoms at any grade (label)
decisionRules.recommendation: Suspend dosing until MRI shows radiographic resolution and symptoms, if present, resolve. Consider a follow-up MRI 2 to 4 months after initial identification. Resumption is guided by clinical judgment.
evidenceNote: Leqembi PI Table 3 and footnote 3, p.7; Kisunla PI Table 2 and footnote b, p.6

decisionRules.recommendation: May continue dosing (Kisunla: at current dose and schedule).
evidenceNote: Leqembi PI Table 4, p.7; Kisunla PI Table 3, p.6

decisionRules.condition: ARIA-H moderate on MRI, or mild or moderate ARIA-H with symptoms (label)
decisionRules.recommendation: Suspend dosing until MRI shows radiographic stabilization and symptoms, if present, resolve. Resumption is guided by clinical judgment. Consider a follow-up MRI 2 to 4 months after initial identification.
evidenceNote: Leqembi PI Table 4 and footnote 2, p.7; Kisunla PI Table 3 and footnote a, p.6

decisionRules.condition: ARIA-H severe on MRI, any symptoms (label)
decisionRules.recommendation: Suspend dosing until MRI shows radiographic stabilization and symptoms, if present, resolve. Use clinical judgment in considering whether to continue or permanently discontinue.
evidenceNote: Leqembi PI Table 4 and footnote 3, p.7; Kisunla PI Table 3 and footnote b, p.6

decisionRules.recommendation: Suspend dosing until MRI shows radiographic stabilization and symptoms, if present, resolve. Use clinical judgment in considering whether to continue after stabilization and symptom resolution or permanently discontinue.
evidenceNote: Leqembi PI §2.4, p.7; Kisunla PI §2.3, p.6

decisionRules.recommendation: Use clinical judgment in considering whether to continue dosing.
evidenceNote: Leqembi PI §5.1, p.13; Kisunla PI §5.1, p.11
Leqembi PI: no experience continuing through symptomatic ARIA-E or asymptomatic radiographically severe ARIA-E

decisionRules.condition: Radiographically severe ARIA-E or ARIA-H, or severe symptoms at any grade (AUR)
decisionRules.recommendation: Discontinue.
evidenceNote: Donanemab AUR §5.4 and Table 8, pp.10–11; §5.6, p.12
Lecanemab AUR p.10 (text) and Table 8, p.30. Its Fig 2 shows a suspend path for asymptomatic severe ARIA

decisionRules.recommendation: Discontinue for: severe radiographic ARIA, severe symptomatic ARIA, any macrohemorrhage, >10 microhemorrhages since starting, more than 1 area of superficial siderosis (AUR text says 1 area), more than 2 ARIA episodes, or any condition requiring an anticoagulant.

Discontinue for: severe radiographic ARIA-E or ARIA-H, any macrohemorrhage, >10 new microhemorrhages since starting, more than 1 area of superficial siderosis, a third ARIA event even if mild and asymptomatic, a seriously symptomatic episode, or a new indication for an anticoagulant. If only 1 area of siderosis emerges, re-evaluate risk and benefit.

Donanemab AUR: resume if symptoms have fully resolved, ARIA-E has resolved, ARIA-H has stabilized, stopping rules are not met, and the patient and care partners want to continue. Lecanemab AUR: once symptoms and ARIA-E resolve, consider restarting after a risk-benefit discussion.
Consider early high-dose glucocorticoid: methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 5 days, then oral taper over several weeks (AUR only; not in either label)
evidenceNote: Lecanemab AUR p.10; donanemab AUR §5.5, p.11

decisionRules.condition: Patient on lecanemab or donanemab needs an anticoagulant or antithrombotic (label)
decisionRules.recommendation: Use additional caution when starting an antithrombotic or thrombolytic. Caution is also advised for patients who need to be on an anticoagulant.
evidenceNote: Leqembi PI §5.1, p.11; Kisunla PI §5.1, p.10

decisionRules.condition: Patient on lecanemab or donanemab needs an anticoagulant (AUR)
decisionRules.recommendation: Stop the antibody. Lecanemab AUR: reinstate if anticoagulation is no longer medically indicated. Donanemab AUR: discontinue.

initialSteps: Symptoms suggestive of ARIA: clinical evaluation including MRI (both labels)

Serious or severe ARIA: MRI promptly with DWI to exclude ischemic stroke; admission to hospital or a critical care unit with staff experienced in cerebral edema may be needed (lecanemab AUR p.10; donanemab AUR §5.5)
Seizures: monitor and treat if they occur (lecanemab AUR p.10); see acute-neuro:convulsive-status-epilepticus
Steroids for serious or severe ARIA: see the steroid rule (AUR only)
disposition: Serious or severe ARIA: hospital or critical care unit may be needed (AURs)
Resumption after a suspension is guided by clinical judgment (labels); AUR conditions are in the resume rule
Follow-up MRI schedule: see the Follow-up MRI row
institutionVaries: Who prescribes and runs the infusion program, and who is called when a dose is suspended
Emergent MRI access, scanner field strength, and who reads ARIA
Level of care for severe ARIA (ward vs ICU)
Whether a written serious-ARIA protocol exists (AURs ask prescribing centers to have one)
pearls: Timing: most ARIA-E radiographic events occur early, within the first 7 doses for lecanemab (Study 2) and the first 24 weeks for donanemab (Study 1); ARIA can occur at any time and patients can have more than 1 episode (PIs §5.1)
Lecanemab Study 2: ARIA-E resolved on MRI in 52% by 12 weeks, 81% by 17 weeks, 100% overall after detection (Leqembi PI §5.1, p.13)
Donanemab Study 1: ARIA-E resolved on MRI in 63% by 12 weeks, 80% by 20 weeks, 83% overall after the first event; symptoms resolved in about 85% (Kisunla PI §5.1, pp.8, 11)

ApoE ε4, lecanemab Study 2: ARIA in homozygotes 45%, heterozygotes 19%, noncarriers 13% (placebo 22%, 9%, 4%); symptomatic ARIA-E 9%, 2%, 1%; serious ARIA 3%, about 1%, about 1%; severe radiographic ARIA-E 5%, 0.4%, 0%; severe ARIA-H 13.5%, 2.1%, 1.1% (Leqembi PI §5.1, pp.11, 13)

ApoE ε4, donanemab Study 1: ARIA in homozygotes 55%, heterozygotes 36%, noncarriers 25% (placebo 22%, 13%, 12%); symptomatic ARIA-E 8%, 7%, 4%; serious ARIA 3%, 2%, 1%; severe ARIA-E 3%, 2%, 0.4%; severe ARIA-H 22%, 8%, 4% (Kisunla PI §5.1, pp.9–11)
ICH >1 cm: lecanemab 0.7% (6/898) vs 0.1% on placebo (Study 2); donanemab 0.5% vs 0.2% on placebo (Study 1) and 1% (Study 2). Fatal ICH has occurred on both (PIs §5.1)

Antithrombotics, lecanemab Study 2: ICH >1 cm 0.9% (3/328) with any antithrombotic vs 0.6% (3/545) without; 2.5% (2/79) on an anticoagulant alone or with an antiplatelet or aspirin vs none on placebo (Leqembi PI §5.1, p.11)
Antithrombotics, donanemab Study 1: ICH >1 cm 0.6% (2/349) with vs 0.4% (2/504) without; ARIA-H 30% vs 29% (Kisunla PI §5.1, p.10)
Fatal ICH has followed thrombolytic use in patients with ARIA symptoms on anti-amyloid antibodies (both PIs §5.1)
Seizure and status epilepticus can occur with ARIA (both PIs §5.1). With severe ARIA, encephalopathy, stupor and lateralizing signs can also occur (lecanemab AUR p.10)
In trials 74%–97% of ARIA was asymptomatic and found on routine MRI (ASNR 2025 p.24)

entries.title: Suspected monogenic small vessel disease (CADASIL and others)
keyNumbers: CADASIL scale (0–25) ≥15: test NOTCH3
NOTCH3: small-vessel stroke <55 y, few risk factors
CBS deficiency: homocysteine often >100 µmol/L
Fabry pulvinar T1 sign: ~23% of hemizygous males
entries.consultQuestion: Unexplained small vessel disease on MRI in a young patient: is it monogenic, which gene, what to send?
keyHistory: Family history across generations: stroke, dementia, migraine with aura, mood disorder; consanguinity
A negative family history does not exclude: de novo variants, mild or misdiagnosed relatives (Manini 2023 p.782; EAN 2020 p.918)
Stroke or hemorrhage before 50 y, recurrent, no common cause (Manini 2023 Table 5)
Hemorrhage after trauma, exertion or an anticoagulant (COL4A1/2)
Hair loss in adolescence, back pain or disc disease, muscle cramps, acroparesthesias, visual or hearing loss
Kidney disease, hematuria, early cataract, infantile hemiparesis in the patient or relatives
keyExam: Skin: angiokeratomas (genital, umbilical), livedo racemosa, yellowish papules on the lateral neck and flexures, early alopecia
Eyes: refer for slit lamp and fundus (see workup)
Build: tall, long limbs, without joint hypermobility (homocystinuria)
redFlags: Family history
Young age at onset
Consanguinity
Extracerebral or systemic features
Imaging or clinical phenotype characteristic of a specific monogenic disease

clues: WMH in anterior temporal poles, external capsules and superior frontal gyrus (Manini 2023 Table 4, p.778)
Migraine with aura (mean onset 30 y), subcortical infarcts, mood disorder, dementia; ischemic stroke mean 49 y, range 20–70 (AHA 2023 p.e452)
Little or no systemic involvement (AHA 2023 Table 1)
ICH rare, especially on anticoagulants (EAN 2020 Table 1)
Lacunar strokes from 20–44 y; scalp alopecia in adolescence in 90%; severe back pain with lumbar disc herniation, spondylosis (EAN 2020 p.919)
Arc sign: T2 hyperintensity from pons to middle cerebellar peduncles, late stage, 5 of 7 patients (Nozaki 2015 pp.460, 462)
Early: frontal white matter and external capsule (Nozaki 2015 p.462)
Like CARASIL but later: stroke onset around 60 y; alopecia and spondylosis less frequent (EAN 2020 p.920)
Deep ICH, spontaneous or after trauma, exertion or an anticoagulant; mean stroke onset 30–40 y; hemorrhagic twice as often as ischemic (EAN 2020 p.921)
Porencephaly, infantile hemiparesis (Manini 2023 pp.774, 781)
Eye: retinal arteriolar tortuosity, cataract (often bilateral and congenital), anterior segment dysgenesis (Axenfeld-Rieger) (Manini 2023 p.775)
Hematuria, renal cysts, muscle cramps with raised CK, intracranial aneurysms (Manini 2023 pp.775, 781)
Microbleeds in more than 50% (Manini 2023 p.781)
Recurrent ischemic strokes from 35–45 y with multiple pontine lacunes (Verdura 2016 p.748)
No cerebral hemorrhage, no extraneurological features; microbleeds in 3 of 12 (Verdura 2016 pp.748–749)
Hematuria or large bilateral renal cysts; muscle cramps with raised CK; retinal arteriolar tortuosity with retinal hemorrhages (Plaisier 2007 pp.2689–2691)
Aneurysms of the intracranial internal carotid; Raynaud phenomenon; supraventricular arrhythmia (Plaisier 2007 pp.2689–2691)
Progressive retinal vasculopathy in almost all symptomatic patients; brain disease from the fourth to fifth decade (EAN 2020 p.923)
Rim-enhancing mass lesion with edema (pseudotumor); white matter calcification on CT in 52% (EAN 2020 p.923)
Kidney, liver and thyroid disease; Raynaud; GI bleeding (EAN 2020 p.923; AHA 2023 Table 1)

differential.dx: Fabry disease (GLA, X-linked; women can be affected)
clues: Acroparesthesias and pain crises, hypohidrosis, angiokeratomas, cornea verticillata, proteinuria, left ventricular hypertrophy (Manini 2023 pp.771, 774–775)
Small vessel, large vessel and cardioembolic infarcts (AHA 2023 Table 1); stroke onset 20–50 y, posterior circulation, basilar dolichoectasia (EAN 2020 p.924)
Pulvinar T1 hyperintensity: 22 of 94 hemizygous males (about 23%); not seen before the third decade (Moore 2003 pp.1097–1098)
Pulvinar sign usually comes with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and severe renal dysfunction (Manini 2023 p.781)
Therapy-resistant hypertension, sicca syndrome (Manini 2023 p.774)
Brainstem symptoms: tinnitus, hearing loss, dysphagia (AHA 2023 Table 1)
WMH in brainstem and frontoparietal white matter with temporal lobes spared (Manini 2023 Table 4, p.781)
Ischemic stroke onset in the seventh decade (Manini 2023 p.769); fewer than 20 cases reported (AHA 2023 Table 1)

differential.dx: Hereditary CAA (APP, CST3, ITM2B, TTR; AD)
clues: Recurrent lobar ICH from middle age, usually before 55 y, often with subarachnoid bleeding; progressive dementia (Manini 2023 pp.771, 774)
CST3 (Icelandic): hemorrhages at 20–30 y (Manini 2023 p.771)
TTR: meningeal enhancement of brain and cord, neuropathy, vitreous opacities (Manini 2023 pp.774–775, 781)
ITM2B (familial British dementia): dementia, cerebellar ataxia and spastic tetraparesis from the fifth decade (Manini 2023 p.774)
Mimic: stroke-like episodes, not small vessel disease (EAN 2020 p.925)
Cortical and juxtacortical lesions that do not match a vascular territory and may spread over days to weeks (EAN 2020 p.925)
Headache, vomiting, focal seizures, encephalopathy; ptosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, muscle weakness, lactic acidosis (EAN 2020 p.925)
Mimic: primary microgliopathy, not a vasculopathy (Konno 2018 p.1093)
Frontotemporal dementia-like picture with parkinsonism or pyramidal signs; mean onset 43 y (women 40, men 47) (Konno 2018 p.1094)
Frontoparietal white matter lesions, thin corpus callosum, diffusion-restricted white matter lesions that persist for months, no enhancement (Konno 2018 pp.1095–1096)
CT: very small calcifications beside the frontal horns; pericallosal stepping stone pattern on sagittal views (Konno 2018 p.1096)
Young women with motor onset are misdiagnosed as MS (Konno 2018 p.1094)
Loose fit: vasculitis (polyarteritis nodosa, Sneddon syndrome) (Manini 2023 pp.770, 775)
Lacunes in deep nuclei, brainstem and thalamus without WMH (Manini 2023 p.781)
Livedo racemosa, periodic fever, pure red cell aplasia or other cytopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia (Manini 2023 p.775)
Treatable: TNF inhibitors lower the risk of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke (Lee 2023 p.6)
Loose fit: small and large vessel disease (Manini 2023 p.769)
Yellowish papules on the lateral neck and flexures; retinal peau d'orange and angioid streaks (Manini 2023 p.775)
GI bleeding, angina, claudication; carotid rete mirabile (Manini 2023 pp.770, 775, Table 4)
Loose fit: arterial and venous thromboembolism; the sources describe no small vessel MRI pattern (GeneReviews 2025; Testai 2010)
Ectopia lentis or severe myopia; tall with long limbs, without joint hypermobility (GeneReviews 2025, Suggestive Findings)
Adults can present with a thromboembolic event alone, often cerebrovascular (GeneReviews 2025, Clinical Description)
Treatable: vitamin B6 (about 40% respond), methionine-restricted diet, betaine (GeneReviews 2025, Table 5)

workup.test: Re-read the MRI for a disease pattern
notes: Look at: anterior temporal poles, external capsules, pons and middle cerebellar peduncles, pulvinar on T1, microbleeds, enhancement, mass-like lesions (Manini 2023 Table 4)
Lacunes and microbleeds point to a vascular cause rather than a leukodystrophy (Manini 2023 p.778)
Use a panel when several diseases are possible; test the single variant when the familial variant is known (AHA 2023 p.e456)
CADASIL (Pescini) scale 0–25: ≥15 suggests CADASIL; use it to select patients for NOTCH3 testing (Manini 2023 p.771)
AHA 2023: consider NOTCH3 testing for small vessel stroke before 55 y with few vascular risk factors (normotensive, nondiabetic, nonsmoker) or a family history of CADASIL (Table 3)
Variant of unknown significance: skin biopsy for electron microscopy (GOM) and/or NOTCH3 immunostaining (EAN 2020 p.918)
Anterior temporal WMH are often present but can be absent (EAN 2020 p.918)

workup.test: Fabry: α-galactosidase A activity in leukocytes (men); GLA sequencing (women)
indication: Cryptogenic stroke with acroparesthesias, angiokeratomas, proteinuria or left ventricular hypertrophy
notes: Enzyme activity can be normal in women (Manini 2023 Table 1)

workup.test: Plasma total homocysteine and plasma amino acids (methionine)
notes: CBS deficiency: total homocysteine often >100 µmol/L (normal <15); adult-onset thromboembolic form 50 to >100 µmol/L (GeneReviews 2025, Suggestive Findings, Table 1)
No vitamin B6, including multivitamins, for 2 weeks before the sample (GeneReviews 2025, Suggestive Findings)
High homocysteine with low or normal methionine points to a remethylation defect (MTHFR, cobalamin), not CBS deficiency (GeneReviews 2025, Differential Diagnosis)

workup.test: m.3243A>G (urine where possible), then POLG sequencing
notes: Muscle biopsy if both are negative (EAN 2020 p.925)
Lactate in blood, CSF or MR spectroscopy supports the diagnosis but is neither specific nor highly sensitive (EAN 2020 Table 1)
Diagnosis of a stroke-like episode needs clinical assessment, MRI and EEG (EAN 2020 p.925)

indication: Suspected Fabry, COL4A1/2, HANAC, RVCL-S, pseudoxanthoma elasticum or homocystinuria
notes: Cornea verticillata (Fabry); retinal arteriolar tortuosity (COL4A1/2, HANAC); retinal vasculopathy (RVCL-S); angioid streaks (pseudoxanthoma elasticum); ectopia lentis (homocystinuria) (Manini 2023 p.775; EAN 2020 p.923; GeneReviews 2025)

indication: Suspected COL4A1/2, HANAC, Fabry or RVCL-S
notes: Hematuria, proteinuria, renal cysts, raised CK (EAN 2020 p.921; Plaisier 2007 pp.2689–2691)

workup.test: CT head, 1 mm sections with sagittal reconstruction
notes: CSF1R calcifications are very small and easily overlooked (Konno 2018 p.1096)
Aneurysms of the intracranial carotid, middle cerebral and basilar arteries (COL4A1, HANAC); vertebrobasilar dolichoectasia (Fabry) (Manini 2023 p.781)

indication: Early-onset ischemic strokes with pontine lacunes
notes: Coding-region sequencing of COL4A1 and COL4A2 was negative in the index family (Verdura 2016 p.746)
Also consider in sporadic cases with pontine lacunes and few vascular risk factors (Verdura 2016 p.750)
No predictive testing in children (AHA 2023 p.e455)

workup.test: DADA2: plasma or serum ADA2 enzyme activity; ADA2 sequencing
indication: Cryptogenic ischemic stroke, unexplained brain hemorrhage (including aneurysm) or spinal cord stroke in childhood or early adulthood (Lee 2023 Table 3, statement 3.5)
notes: Near-absent ADA2 activity is diagnostic; normal activity excludes DADA2 (Lee 2023 Table 2, statement 2.3)
Biallelic pathogenic or likely pathogenic ADA2 variants are diagnostic; one variant means a carrier (Lee 2023 Table 2, statements 2.4–2.5)
Standard sequencing can miss intronic, regulatory and copy-number variants; if suspicion remains, send enzyme activity or further genetic tests (Lee 2023 Table 2, statement 2.7)
ADA2 activity is measured by few laboratories; ADA2 is on most inborn-errors-of-immunity and autoinflammatory panels (Lee 2023 p.4)

decisionRules.condition: Small vessel disease in a patient with conventional vascular risk factors
decisionRules.recommendation: Do not exclude a monogenic cause

decisionRules.condition: Unexplained symmetrical periventricular WMH plus a family history of migraine with aura, stroke, mood disorder or dementia
decisionRules.recommendation: Consider CADASIL

decisionRules.condition: Small vessel stroke before 55 y with few vascular risk factors, or a family history of CADASIL
decisionRules.recommendation: Consider NOTCH3 testing
evidenceNote: AHA 2023 scientific statement, Table 3: ungraded consideration

decisionRules.recommendation: Skin biopsy for electron microscopy and/or NOTCH3 immunostaining

decisionRules.condition: Early scalp alopecia, severe spondylosis, and unexplained early lacunar strokes or symmetrical WMH
decisionRules.recommendation: Consider CARASIL

decisionRules.condition: Deep ICH or WMH of undetermined origin with a first- or second-degree relative who has cerebral hemorrhage, porencephaly, retinal vessel tortuosity, hematuria, renal cysts or insufficiency, infantile hemiparesis, early cataract, anterior segment abnormality, multiple intracranial aneurysms, muscle cramps or a hepatic cyst; or early-onset pontine infarcts
decisionRules.recommendation: Seek a COL4A1 or COL4A2 variant
evidenceNote: Early-onset pontine infarcts are in the text version of the statement (p.921), not in Table 1

decisionRules.condition: Clinical or genetic diagnosis of CADASIL
decisionRules.recommendation: Avoid diagnostic cerebral catheter angiography (relative contraindication); exception: known symptomatic acute large vessel occlusion. 11 of 16 had neurologic symptoms lasting hours to weeks after angiography
evidenceNote: AHA 2023 scientific statement, p.e458 and Table 3: ungraded consideration

decisionRules.recommendation: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant treatment not recommended
IV thrombolysis not recommended

EAN: no thrombolysis unless the stroke is from a large-artery occlusion with a concurrent cause. AHA: safety and efficacy unknown for small vessel stroke, decide case by case; for an unrelated large vessel stroke, thrombectomy without thrombolysis may be preferred
evidenceNote: AHA 2023 scientific statement, p.e456 and Table 3: ungraded consideration
The two documents differ; both are shown

decisionRules.recommendation: Not recommended for stroke prophylaxis; not contraindicated when there is another indication (e.g., atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolus)
evidenceNote: AHA 2023 Table 3 (ungraded): with high-risk atrial fibrillation, appendage occlusion may be preferred to long-term anticoagulation, particularly with a high microbleed burden

decisionRules.recommendation: Systemic thrombolysis is not contraindicated
Fibrinolysis is not indicated
Avoid antiplatelet, anticoagulant and other antithrombotic therapy, to prevent hemorrhagic stroke
evidenceNote: DADA2 consensus 2023 Delphi, statement 5.5: LOE 5 (D), agreement 8.3 of 9 (Lee 2023 Table 5)
Secondary hemorrhagic conversion of stroke has been documented (Lee 2023 p.7)

initialSteps: Complete the standard stroke or ICH etiology workup first: see young-stroke-workup and ich-etiology-workup
Lobar hemorrhage pattern: see boston-criteria-caa
disposition: Genetics referral; offer relatives genetic counseling (EAN 2020 Table 1: mean 4.84, 100%)
Follow-up at a specialized center or with an expert neurologist (EAN 2020 Table 1: mean 4.77, 100%)
Confirmed COL4A1/2 variant: brain MRI, intracranial and cervical MRA, echocardiogram, eye exam with ocular pressure, renal and liver ultrasound, CK (EAN 2020 p.921 and Table 1: mean 4.93, 100%)
institutionVaries: Which panel and laboratory; whether the gene list covers HTRA1, COL4A1/2 including the 3′UTR, TREX1, CTSA, CSF1R and ADA2
Mitochondrial DNA testing route and sample type
α-galactosidase A assay availability and turnaround
Genetics referral route and inpatient versus outpatient testing
pearls: CADASIL has been diagnosed as MS; the corpus callosum can be involved (EAN 2020 p.918)
Fewer than 2% of younger-onset lacunar strokes are genetically confirmed CADASIL (AHA 2023 p.e452)
Fabry disease explains less than 1% of cryptogenic ischemic strokes in young adults (EAN 2020 p.925)
Monogenic small vessel diseases cause 1%–5% of all strokes (Manini 2023 p.766)
Sources disagree on migraine frequency in CADASIL: about 30% (AHA 2023 p.e452) and up to 45% (Manini 2023 p.771)

Red flags above are EAN 2020 Delphi consensus items (Table 1): family history mean 5 (100%); young onset 4.92 (100%); consanguinity 4.92 (100%); extracerebral features 4.54 (100%); characteristic phenotype 4.54 (84.6%) and 4.61 (92.8%)

entries.title: Functional neurological disorder (FND): positive signs
entries.consultQuestion: Could this be functional — which positive signs make the diagnosis, and what still needs excluding?
keyNumbers: Hoover sign: sens 60–100%, spec 86–100%
Drift without pronation: spec 100%
Functional seizure clue: duration >90 s
Comorbid neurological disease in ~20%
New explanation at 18 mo: 4 of 1,030
keyHistory: Witness account, or a phone video of a typical attack — expert review of a video may be enough (Bennett 2021; Dworetzky 2025)
Memory of the event favours a functional seizure (Bennett 2021)
keyExam: Hoover sign and hip abductor sign — the most reliable signs of functional leg weakness (Bennett 2021)
Hoover sign: sensitivity 60–100%, specificity 86–100%; valid for unilateral leg weakness with no lesion in the opposite SMA or parietal lobe (Dworetzky 2025, Table 2)
Give-way (collapsing) weakness: sensitivity 20–90%, specificity 95–100%; beware pain or difficulty following instructions (Dworetzky 2025, Table 2; Bennett 2021)
Drift without pronation (palms up, wait 10 s): sensitivity 47–93%, specificity 100% (Dworetzky 2025, Table 2)
Tremor entrainment: tap the other hand at different rates — functional tremor stops, entrains or disrupts the copying (sensitivity 89.5%, specificity 100%) (Dworetzky 2025, Table 2; Bennett 2021)
Dragging leg gait: sensitivity 20–100%, specificity 100% (Dworetzky 2025, Table 2)
redFlags: Post-ictal confusion or stertorous breathing — favour an epileptic seizure (Bennett 2021)
Stereotyped, brief, clustered events, or events from EEG-proven sleep — consider frontal lobe seizures (Dworetzky 2025, Table 2)
Midline-splitting sensory loss is not reliable — seen with thalamic stroke (Dworetzky 2025, Table 2)

differential.dx: Epileptic seizures, including frontal lobe seizures
clues: Some frontal lobe seizures have a normal ictal EEG (Bennett 2021)
Pelvic thrusting and asynchronous movements also occur in frontal lobe seizures (Dworetzky 2025)
About 20% of FND patients have one (Bennett 2021)
Functional tremor can occur in early Parkinson's disease (Bennett 2021)
Symptoms can look functional before another disorder emerges (Dworetzky 2025)

notes: Still the gold standard (Dworetzky 2025)
A smartphone recording with expert review may be enough (Dworetzky 2025; Bennett 2021)

decisionRules.recommendation: Diagnose on positive 'rule in' signs, not by excluding every other cause (DSM-5, 2013)

decisionRules.condition: Eye closure with prolonged side-to-side movements and a negative ictal EEG
decisionRules.recommendation: Epileptic seizure very unlikely — but comorbid functional seizures and epilepsy are not excluded

initialSteps: Tell the patient what it is, not what it isn't: 'You have FND for the following reasons: a, b and c' (Bennett 2021, Table 1)
Show how the diagnosis was made, e.g. demonstrate the Hoover sign (Dworetzky 2025, Table 3)
Mention the diagnosis as soon as history and exam give reasonable suspicion (Dworetzky 2025)
institutionVaries: Access to video-EEG and to FND therapy services (physiotherapy, psychotherapy)
pearls: Ictal eye closure: sensitivity 34–88%, specificity 74–100% (Dworetzky 2025, Table 2)
Ictal weeping: specificity 100% but sensitivity 3.7–37% — confirm it wasn't postictal (Dworetzky 2025, Table 2)
Side-to-side head or body movement (convulsive events only): sensitivity 25–63%, specificity 96–100% (Dworetzky 2025, Table 2)
Urinary incontinence and injury are poor discriminators (Bennett 2021)
Misdiagnosis is rare: 4 of 1,030 had a better explanation at 18 months, and twice as many were misdiagnosed the other way (Bennett 2021)
Table 2 figures are Dworetzky 2025's adaptation of Aybek & Perez BMJ 2022
